Maladaptive Strategies.value: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
I try to erase the memory of the event
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette:
Valentina Reyes is a 38-year-old Salvadoran American woman who works as a community organizer in a mid-sized city in the Southwest, coordinating tenant rights campaigns and neighborhood advocacy efforts. She came to the clinic after her partner, noticing months of sleeplessness and emotional distance, gently insisted she speak to someone. Valentina agreed, though she arrived at the first session with the quiet wariness of someone who had spent decades convincing herself she did not need to.

The history she offered was careful and partial, offered in pieces. Growing up in a household where her stepfather's rages were unpredictable and her mother's attention was unreliable, Valentina had learned early to read rooms and people. The abuse was physical and sustained across several years of her childhood - beatings that could be triggered by something as ordinary as a door left open or a plate set down too loudly. What she returned to most often in session was one particular incident, perhaps when she was nine or ten: being cornered in the kitchen, the counter at her back, her stepfather blocking the only exit, the sensation of having absolutely nowhere to go. She could recall certain images from that moment with a sharpness that startled her - the pattern of the linoleum, the color of his shirt - while other parts of the memory were simply absent, as if someone had cut them from the reel. At other times she could narrate the event with a flat, factual calm that unnerved even her, describing it as though it had happened to a girl she once read about rather than to herself.

In the years that followed, Valentina built a life that looked, from the outside, like one of remarkable resilience. She was good at her work - genuinely good - and she threw herself into it with an intensity that left little room for anything else. Her calendar was always full. When a difficult memory surfaced without warning during a meeting or while drafting a report, she learned to push harder into the task in front of her, to bury the intrusion under the weight of action. Her colleagues admired her drive. What they did not see was that she was also, in every meeting room and community center she entered, quietly scanning for where to sit. She chose her chair the way someone might choose a position in enemy territory: back against the wall, full view of the door, no one behind her. If the only available seat placed her back to the room, she would wait, or rearrange, or make an excuse. In her work, which required constant presence in unfamiliar spaces - church halls, apartment lobbies, city council chambers - this was not a minor inconvenience. There were organizing sessions she left early, coalition meetings where she could not focus because the seating arrangement felt wrong, moments where her attention was less on the agenda than on who was moving behind her.

She had come to believe, with a certainty that sat beneath her conscious reasoning, that a stronger person would have found a way out of that kitchen. Someone else would have done something - screamed louder, run faster, fought back. That she had not was, in her private accounting, evidence of something fundamentally insufficient in her. This belief coexisted with a numbness she described as feeling dead inside, a flatness that settled over her particularly in moments of intimacy or stillness. Her partner had noticed it. Valentina had noticed it too, and found it frightening in a way she struggled to articulate - as though the emotional life she was supposed to have was operating behind glass.

At night, the vigilance that she managed to channel into productivity during the day had nowhere to go. She lay awake listening, certain that relaxing her attention entirely was not safe, though she could not always say what she was listening for. The exhaustion was accumulating.

What finally brought her in was a community meeting three months ago in which a tenant described being trapped in a lease with no legal recourse, no options, no way out. Valentina had felt something shift dangerously inside her and had excused herself to stand in the parking lot until it passed. She came to therapy hoping, she said, to feel something real again. What she feared most was that she no longer could.
